points.text: angle (subtended at the centre of a circle) when arc (length) = radius

markScheme.note: This MS uses B1/C1/A1 mark codes (B = independent mark, C = method/calculation mark, A = answer mark after a C mark), not the biology-style ;/A/R/I shorthand. Codes are kept in a 'code' field on each point and shown as printed.

explanation.text: The radian is defined by comparing an arc to the radius: if you mark off an arc on a circle whose length equals the radius, the angle at the centre subtended by that arc is exactly 1 radian. This is why angle in radians = arc length ÷ radius.

reasoningChain: State the geometric relationship: arc length = radius defines 1 radian at the centre.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing radian only as a 'unit of angle' without the arc-equals-radius condition, which the ER flags as the commonly missing part of the definition.

stem.text: Three children are playing on a roundabout (rotatable horizontal platform) at a playground. Child X is standing on the edge of the roundabout. This child is pushing so that the edge of the roundabout moves in a circle at a constant speed of 2.4 m s<sup>–1</sup>, as shown in the view from above in Figure 1.1.

stem.caption: Figure 1.1
stem.alt: View from above of a circular roundabout rotating anticlockwise (labelled 'rotation' with a curved arrow). The centre has a small circle. Three children are marked with dots on radial lines from the centre: Z at distance R from the centre, Y at distance 2R from the centre, and X on the edge of the roundabout, which has radius 3R. An arrow at X labelled 2.4 m s–1 shows the direction of motion, tangential to the edge.

stem.text: The radius of the roundabout is 3R. Child Y is sitting on the roundabout at a distance 2R from the centre. Child Z is sitting at a distance R from the centre.
stem.note:
QP prints these three sentences as separate short lines under the figure; rendered here as one text block to preserve the line breaks with
would be more faithful, keeping as plain sentences since no answer line follows each.

stem.text: Child Y is moving in a circle with an angular speed of 0.75 rad s<sup>–1</sup>.

explanation.text: Child Y moves at distance 2R from the centre with angular speed ω = 0.75 rad s⁻¹. Y's linear speed equals X's linear speed (2.4 m s⁻¹) only if Y is at the edge — but Y is at 2R, not 3R. Instead, use v = rω with Y's own linear speed. Y's linear speed isn't given directly in m s⁻¹; but since X is on the edge (radius 3R) moving at 2.4 m s⁻¹, and Y and X share the same ω (they're on the same rigid rotating platform), you can find ω from X first: ω = v_X / (3R)... but R is unknown. The MS shortcuts this by applying v = rω directly to Y's own data (Y's radius is 2R, but the MS solves for the roundabout's radius 3R algebraically): since all points on the roundabout share ω, and v_X = 2.4 m s⁻¹ at radius 3R, while Y has angular speed 0.75 rad s⁻¹ at radius 2R, and these describe the same ω, so ω = 0.75 rad s⁻¹ for the whole platform. Applying v = rω to X: 2.4 = (3R)(0.75), giving 3R = 2.4/0.75 = 3.2 m, which is the roundabout's radius.

reasoningChain: All points on a rotating rigid platform share the same angular speed ω.
Y's angular speed (0.75 rad s⁻¹) is therefore also X's angular speed.
Apply v = rω to X, where r = 3R is the roundabout's radius and v = 2.4 m s⁻¹: 3R = v/ω = 2.4/0.75 = 3.2 m.

inferredMistakes.text: Using R = v/ω directly without multiplying by 3, giving 1.6 m (the radius at X's own position confused with R), or multiplying by 2 instead of 3 giving 4.8 m — both flagged by the ER as common wrong answers from confusing how R relates to the roundabout's actual radius 3R.

stem.text: the frequency of rotation of the roundabout

explanation.text: The whole roundabout shares one angular speed ω = 0.75 rad s⁻¹ (established in b(i)). Frequency of rotation relates to ω by ω = 2πf, so f = ω/2π, independent of which child's radius you look at.

reasoningChain: Use ω = 2πf with the shared angular speed ω = 0.75 rad s⁻¹.

inferredMistakes.text: Treating angular frequency as different for each child (e.g. trying to recompute ω from Y's radius again), when ω is the same for every point on a rigid rotating platform.

stem.text: the centripetal acceleration of child Y.

markScheme.note: The MS computes Y's radius as 3.2 × ⅔ (since Y is at 2R and the roundabout's radius 3R = 3.2 m, so 2R = 3.2 × 2/3).

explanation.text: Centripetal acceleration a = rω² needs Y's own radius (2R), not the roundabout's radius (3R). Since 3R = 3.2 m (from b(i)), 2R = 3.2 × (2/3) = 2.13 m. Then a = 2.13 × 0.75² ≈ 1.2 m s⁻².

reasoningChain: Apply a = rω² using Y's radius and the shared ω = 0.75 rad s⁻¹.

inferredMistakes.text: Using the roundabout's radius 3R (3.2 m) instead of Y's own radius 2R, which the ER notes as candidates not realising the radius at Y's position is two-thirds of the roundabout's radius.

stem.text: For the roundabout in 1(b), complete Table 1.1 to compare the linear and angular velocities for child X and child Z at any instant in time. Indicate your response by placing one tick (✓) in the appropriate box for each of magnitude and direction for the two quantities.

stem.caption: Table 1.1
head: magnitude
direction
stem.note: QP prints a blank grid of tick boxes under two grouped headers ('magnitude' with 3 sub-columns, 'direction' with 2 sub-columns); reproduced here as a header row plus the sub-column labels, with the two data rows left blank for the student to tick.

points.text: linear velocity magnitude: X greater than Z
angular velocity: magnitude equal and direction same

explanation.text: Angular velocity (ω) is the same for every point on a rigid rotating body, so X and Z (both on the roundabout) have equal angular velocity magnitude, and since they rotate together as one rigid body, the same rotational sense gives the same direction convention. Linear velocity v = rω depends on radius: X is at 3R (further out) than Z is at R, so X has the larger linear speed. For direction, X and Z sit on opposite sides of the centre at any instant shown (the figure shows them on different radii from the same centre, roughly diametrically placed relative to each other in this configuration), so their instantaneous linear velocity vectors point in opposite directions.

reasoningChain: Linear speed v = rω scales with radius: X (3R) has greater linear speed than Z (R).
At the positions shown in Figure 1.1, X and Z's velocity vectors point in opposite directions.
Angular velocity (both magnitude and direction/sense of rotation) is identical for every point on a rigid rotating body.

inferredMistakes.text: Ticking 'X less than Z' for linear velocity magnitude by confusing angular speed (equal for both) with linear speed (which depends on radius).

issues.note: QP prints 'The radius of the roundabout is 3R. / Child Y is sitting... / Child Z is sitting...' as three separate short sentences, each on its own line, with no bullet markers. Combined into one text block rather than three separate blocks since they form one short descriptive passage immediately preceding the calculation prompt; no answer lines or bullets attach to them individually.

The printed table has two grouped column headers ('magnitude' spanning 3 tick-columns, 'direction' spanning 2 tick-columns) with empty tick boxes in the two data rows. Represented as a flat table with the sub-column labels in the header row; the grouping structure (magnitude/direction spanning multiple columns) is not separately encoded in the site's table schema.
